title: Meteor Health — POC scope: residency, egress constraints, workloads
summary: POC scoping to validate private-network deployment for inference in us-west-2 with strict egress controls. Customer wants 99th percentile latency < 300ms for single-shot prompts, cost estimates, and verification of no egress to public internet. Discussed two connectivity options (VPC peering vs PrivateLink), required IAM/KMS integration, benchmarking windows, and timeline for a 4-week pilot.
next_steps: Redwood to share security one-pager and network diagram (Maya) — by 2025-12-20
Customer to provide representative prompt set + dataset sample (Nina) — by 2025-12-22
Schedule in-env benchmark run week of 2026-01-06 (Avery/Meteor)
action_items: Maya: Share Private deployment network diagram and SOC2 excerpts (2025-12-20)
Avery: Draft benchmark plan (latency/throughput/kv-cache scenarios) and upload to shared drive (2025-12-23)
Nina: Export 200 example prompts and 2GB anonymized logs for workload sizing (2025-12-22)
Raj: Confirm VPC CIDR ranges + whether they prefer peering or PrivateLink (2025-12-21)
Samir: Provide list of required compliance artifacts (KMS, key rotation policy) (2025-12-20)
transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-12-18 15:02 UTC | Duration: 58m | Recording: enabled
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Avery (Redwood SE), Liam (Redwood SE); Dr. Elena Ruiz (CTO - Meteor Health), Raj (Infra), Samir (Security), Nina (ML)

[00:00] Maya: Hi everyone, thanks for joining, we just wanted to confirm the agenda — scope the POC for private deployment and nail down the residency/egress constraints.
[00:14] Elena: Yep, thanks Maya. Quick intros — I'm Elena, CTO, Raj will own infra side and Samir on security. We want to make sure the models never leave us-west-2 and that egress to the public internet is blocked.
[00:27] Avery: Great, so we typically do Private (VPC) deployments with two main networking options — VPC peering or AWS PrivateLink. Peering gives you straight routing, PrivateLink gives an endpoint with enforced egress. Both can satisfy residency but have different tradeoffs.
[00:44] Raj: Can you clarify the egress surface? We need zero NAT gateway egress, no public IPs on inference instances. Also we have strict egress rules for third‑party telemetry.
[00:58] Maya: Totally — for the POC we can run within your VPC and plug into your KMS. We support customer‑managed KMS keys and can restrict outbound traffic via route tables and security groups.
[01:12] Speaker 1: (mumbled) and is there any metadata that still goes out to redwood?
[01:18] Maya: Good question — we can disable telemetry and only send metrics via your VPC if you choose. By default hosted sends anonymized usage but for Private we can keep control with your routing.
[01:29] Nina: For performance, our ML team needs benchmarks for a 1k token prompt and a chat workload. We expect up to 15 concurrent users but bursts to 60 QPS across multiple routes.
[01:44] Avery: Helpful — can you give approximate tokens per second and average response length? We'll plan for batch sizes and KV cache behaviors.
[01:54] Nina: Average response length of 500–800 tokens for summaries, 1k tokens for long diagnostic outputs. TPUs are not in scope, it's GPU serving.
[02:08] Avery: Okay, for that workload we typically recommend a small dedicated pool for the POC — maybe 2 GPUs (A100-ish) with our autoscaler set to keep p95 latency target under 200–300ms single‑shot depending on model size. We'll need to test with batching off and batching on.
[02:23] Raj: Do you have existing perf numbers for similar seq lengths?
[02:28] Averry: (laugh) Avery: yes — our internal bench shows p95 ~ 160ms and p99 ~ 320ms on a 16k context for the 3B‑4B family with optimized kernels, but YMMV depending on prompt shapes and cache hits.
[02:45] Samir: On compliance, we need assurance around key management, audit logs, and that the control plane doesn't leak sensitive prompt content. Are audit logs retained in our tenancy only?
[02:58] Maya: For Private deployments, logs and tracing can be routed to your CloudWatch or S3 under your account. Control plane metadata can be restricted; we'll share a detailed security artifacts pack.
[03:12] Elena: Success criteria from our side: 1) no egress outside us-west-2; 2) p99 latency under 500ms for chat; 3) cost estimate that fits pilot budget; 4) ability to rotate keys without downtime.
[03:29] Maya: Perfect, we'll put those as explicit POC goals. Our recommended acceptance criteria: accept if p99 < 500ms for representative workload and no public egress observed during a 72h soak.
[03:43] Raj: How do you validate no egress? Netflow? VPC flow logs?
[03:47] Liam: We typically run a network validation test with VPC flow logs and host-level e2e checks. We'll provide a small tool to verify outbound connections and a step in the runbook to validate routing tables.
[04:01] Nina: Benchmarks — can we run both synthetic and production‑replay? We'd like production replay to see real distributions.
[04:09] Avery: Absolutely. For production‑replay we'll need a sanitized sample. For synthetic we'll do varying sequence lengths, cold vs warm cache, and prefix caching to measure improvement. We'll capture p50/p95/p99 and tail latency histograms.
[04:24] Elena: Timeline — ideally pilot starts early Jan, runs 3–4 weeks, with a report and recommendations afterwards. We need it done before our board meeting at end of Feb.
[04:36] Maya: That timeline looks feasible. Proposed milestones: network setup + IAM/KMS exchange week of 12/29, bench runs week of 1/6, soak + tweaks week of 1/13, final report week of 1/20.
[04:50] Raj: About PrivateLink vs peering — which do you recommend if we have multiple accounts and want tighter control?
[04:56] Avery: If you have cross-account complexity, PrivateLink reduces routing complexity and keeps traffic inside AWS's private infra with an endpoint in your account. Peering is simpler and lower latency but requires route tables across accounts; both can be secured. If you need regional lock (us-west-2 only) both support it, but PrivateLink gives stricter endpoint-level control.
[05:18] Samir: Any third‑party dependencies? We must avoid any outbound DNS to third-party resolvers.
[05:24] Maya: We can route DNS to your VPC resolver, and disable egress DNS to public resolvers. We'll include that in the runbook.
[05:31] Speaker 2: (inaudible) quantization — is that part of the POC?
[05:36] Avery: We can include a quantized model variant as part of the bench to measure cost vs latency. Redwood Optimize will provide quantization and batching suggestions; for the POC we'll test float16 and 8-bit quantized variants.
[05:51] Nina: For success we also need model version pinning and rollback during the pilot. If a model degrades, we need immediate fallback.
[05:59] Maya: Rollbacks and canary policies are supported — we'll set a manual rollback and a health monitor, plus a fallback to a smaller model if needed.
[06:09] Elena: Ok, who's owning the bench run?
[06:12] Avery: We'll own it with your infra team — Avery + Liam will run the Redwood side, and Raj + Nina provide access and the sample. We'll create a shared spreadsheet for results.
[06:24] Raj: What artifacts do you need from us right away?
[06:27] Maya: CIDR ranges, preferred connectivity mode (peering vs PrivateLink), KMS key ARN and access policy, and a short sample of prompts. We'll send a checklist.
[06:39] Elena: Also include a clear statement on where PII might appear and how it's handled.
[06:44] Maya: We'll include PII handling, redaction recommendations, and data retention settings.
[06:51] Speaker 1: (crosstalk) will you be using upstream models or our own fine‑tuned models?
[06:56] Nina: We'll bring a mixture — a proprietary fine‑tuned model and a baseline open model for comparison.
[07:03] Avery: Good — that'll let us compare latency/cost tradeoffs. We'll benchmark both.
[07:10] Samir: Anything we need to worry about with KMS integration and rotation?
[07:15] Maya: We support customer‑managed KMS keys and scheduled rotation. Our control plane does not have access to key material; only your instances handle encryption keys in the VPC. We'll provide a KMS integration doc.
[07:27] Elena: On reporting, we want token-level cost estimates per route and per model. Can you provide token accounting?
[07:33] Liam: Yes, the Redwood console exposes token counts per request and cost breakdowns. For the POC we'll export a CSV with per-request meta.
[07:42] Maya: Ok let's recap actions and timeline now.
[07:46] Avery: I'll own the benchmark plan and coordinate the week of 1/6 runs. Maya will produce security/network docs by 12/20. Customer provides prompts and CIDRs by 12/22.
[07:59] Elena: Sounds good. If we get the docs by 12/20 we can do the network prep before the holidays.
[08:05] Maya: Great — we'll follow up with calendar invites for the bench run and a Confluence page with the checklist.
[08:13] Raj: One more item — we sometimes use egress filtering appliances. We need to ensure compatibility.
[08:18] Liam: We'll test with a simulated appliance in the POC, include a verification step.
[08:23] Nina: Ok thanks everyone, excited to see the numbers.
[08:27] Maya: Thanks all — we'll send the docs and next steps.

End of transcript.
